review. That some party has petitioned for a rule and the agency has declined 
to begin rulemaking proceedings is not much of a record upon which to premise 
a determination of whether the agency’s action is arbitrary, capricious, or an 
abuse of discretion.
Hence, in the circuit court cases in which refusals to regulate have been 
subjected to review, one often finds that they occur in circumstances in which 
an agency has already committed substantial resources to the relevant 
regulatory question and has developed a record, including a reasoned 
explanation for failure to go forward. In Lyng itself, for example, the petition 
was for an amendment to a preexisting rule that the agency had previously 
described as tentative and subject to revision after further investigation. That 
investigation had been conducted by contracting for extensive studies by 
outside experts. The agency had held meetings and conferences to discuss the 
results of those studies, had drafted new regulations, and had admitted the 
“apparent inconsistency of the current regulation * * * with the law and the 
[subsequent] research.” Even then, the court only remanded the question to 
the Secretary for further explanation of why the rulemaking process was 
aborted.
VQst-Massachusetts v. EPA, lower courts have taken Justice Stevens’s 
narrowing language seriously. Thus, courts have continued to hold that, in the 
absence of apphcable statutory or regulatory standards, agency denials of 
petitions for rulemaking are committed to agency discretion and therefore 
beyond review. See Conservancy of Sw. Fl. v. FWS, 677 F.3d 1073 (11th Cir. 
2012) (refusing to review the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service s decision to deny 
petitions to initiate rulemaking to designate a critical habitat for the Florida 
panther). When courts have exercised review over an agency’s petition denial, 
they have remained extremely deferential. The Second Circuit, for instance, 
has described its standard of review in such situations as “akin to non-
reviewability.” New York v. NEC, 589 F.3d 551, 554 (2d Cir. 2009) (per curiam) 
(quoting Cellnet Common, Inc. v. FCC, 965 F.2d 1106, 1111 (D.C. Cir. 19W 
Thus, when asked to review a U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) 
decision to deny rulemaking petitions filed by Massachusetts and California, 
it “d[id] no more than assure itself that [the] agency’s decision was ‘reason^, 
meaning that it considered the relevant factors.” Id. at 554. Because the NRC 
analyzed the studies submitted by Massachusetts and California in support ot 
their petitions, the court held that the agency had satisfied its statutory duty 
and therefore further review by the court was not appropriate.
In Flyers Rights Educ. Fund, Inc. v. F.A.A., 864 F.3d 738 (D.C. Cir. 201^, 
however, the D.C. Circuit allowed an airline passengers’ rights group to 
challenge the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) denial of its 
a rulemaking to address emergency egress concerns. Judge Patricia 
acknowledged that, while judicial review of agency inaction must be limited, t e 
case warranted review because the FAA had failed to address a critical satety 
issue “smack-dab within [its] regulatory ambit” and done so on the basis o a 
“vacuous” record.
